Building STANDATA | Alberta.ca ©2024 Government of Alberta | Published: April 2024 | STANDATA variance 23-BCV-001 Building Window opening control devices (WOCD) Date Issued: April 2024 Page 1 of 3 Purpose To provide an alternative solution in meeting the requirements of Sentences 9.8.8.1 (4) and (5) Guards on windows of residential occupancy in the National Building Code – 2023 Alberta Edition (NBC (AE)). Discussion The National Building Code - 2023 Alberta Edition introduced a new requirement in Clause 9.8.8.1 (4) (b) and Sentence 9.8.8.1.(5) by requiring a mechanism that can only be released with the use of tools or special knowledge to control the free swinging or sliding operation of all openable windows that are less than 900mm from the ﬁnished ﬂoor and more than 1800mm from the ﬂoor or ground level on the other side of the window. The intention of this requirement is to reduce the probability of young children opening a window greater than 100mm and falling out of that window opening. The Appendix Note A-9.8.8.1 (4) refers to ASTM F2090 “Standard Speciﬁcation for Window Fall Prevention Devices with Emergency Escape (Egress) Release Mechanisms” as a way of providing the protection required in 9.8.8.1 (4) (b) and (5). Also, Sentence 9.9.10.1 (1) requires that each bedroom must have at least one outside window or exterior door openable from the inside without the use of keys, tools, or special knowledge. However, there is no reference under Sentence 9.9.10.1.(1) to ASTM F2090 “Standard Speciﬁcation for Window Fall Prevention Devices with Emergency Escape (Egress) Release Mechanisms” as a means of providing the required window (openable with a minimum dimension of 380mm, and a minimum unobstructed area of .35m²). This variance allows for the installation of a mechanism that complies with ASTM F2090 “Standard Speciﬁcation for Window Fall Prevention Devices with

Emergency Escape (Egress) Release Mechanisms” to be installed. Code References Sentences 9.8.8.1.(4) & (5) 9.8.8.1. Required Guards 4) Except as provided in Sentence (5), openable windows in buildings of residential occupancy shall be protected by a) a guard, or b) a mechanism that can only be released with the use of tools or special knowledge to control the free swinging or sliding operation of the openable part of the window so as to limit any clear unobstructed opening to not more than 100 mm measured either vertically or horizontally. (See Note A-9.8.8.1.(4).) 5) Windows need not be protected in accordance with Sentence (4), where the bottom edge of the openable portion of the window is located a) more than 900 mm above the finished floor, or STANDATA 23-BCV-001 Page 2 of 3 Building STANDATA | Alberta.ca ©2024 Government of Alberta | April 2024 | Municipal Affairs b) less than 1 800 mm above the floor or ground on the other side of the window. (See Note A-9.8.8.1.(4).) A-9.8.8.1.(4) Window Fall Prevention. The primary intent of the requirement is to minimize the likelihood of small children falling significant heights from open windows. Reflecting reported cases, the requirement applies to openable windows in dwelling units and generally those located on the second floor or higher of residential or mixed use buildings. Once cracked open, some openable windows can be opened further by simply pushing on the openable part of the window. Care must be taken in selecting windows, as some with special operating hardware can still be opened further by simply pushing on the window or by deactivating a spring-loaded button or other mechanism that is not considered a window opening control device (WOCD) that could be inadvertently operated by a young child. A technical description of WOCDs can be found in

ASTM F2090, “Standard Specification for Window Fall Prevention Devices With Emergency Escape (Egress) Release Mechanisms.” Examples of WOCDs that can limit window openings to a maximum of 100 mm as required by Clause 9.8.8.1.(4)(b) include, but are not limited to, a fixed-stop lever, a fixed-length cable and a fixed- position stop block. It is important to note that rotary opening mechanisms cannot limit window openings to 100 mm as required by Clause 9.8.8.1.(4)(b) and that windows with such mechanisms cannot act as guards as required by Clause 9.8.8.1.(4)(a), even when the crank handle is removed. Similarly, awning windows with scissor hardware may not keep the window from swinging open once it is unlatched. Hopper windows would be affected only if an opening is created at the bottom as well as at the top of the window. The requirement will impact primarily on the use of sliding windows which do not incorporate devices in their construction that can be used to limit the openable area of the window. The 100 mm opening limit stated in Sentence 9.8.8.1.(4) is recognized as the maximum opening size required to protect small children from falling through open windows. The minimum 900 mm height of the openable portion of windows required by Sentence 9.8.8.1.(5) corresponds to the minimum height of guards required by Sentence 9.8.8.3.(2) as a means of fall protection in residential occupancies. Sentence 9.9.10.1.(1) 9.9.10.1. Egress Windows or Doors for Bedrooms 1) Except where the suite is sprinklered, each bedroom or combination bedroom shall have at least one outside window or exterior door openable from the inside without the use of keys, tools or special knowledge and without the removal of sashes or hardware. (See Article 9.5.1.2. and Note A-9.9.10.1.(1).) Application This variance applies to buildings of residential occupancy covered by Part 9 of

the National Building Code – 2023 Alberta Edition. Discussion Off-site construction of buildings is a process of maximizing the delivery of building products as much as possible as one module/building. Currently it has become a well-suited solution to control project schedules and budgets while controlling quality and reducing environmental impact. Method of off-site review by registered professionals and/or inspections by the authority having jurisdiction (AHJ) achieves a minimum level of performance as required by the NBC(AE) in areas defined by the code objectives. Additionally, functional statements on the acceptable solution may be considered as an alternative to achieving code compliance. CSA-A660 “Certification of manufacturers of steel building systems” may be recognized for completed steel building modules. An additional letter of assurance by a registered professional or permit service report by an AHJ will be required for any installation of building services. (i.e., electrical, plumbing, HVAC, building envelope). Code References Division C, Article 2.5.1.1. 2.5.1 Factory-Built Assemblies 2.5.1.1. Building STANDATA | Alberta.ca ©2024 Government of Alberta | Published: May 2024 | Municipal Affairs STANDATA variance 23-BCV-003 Building Insulation below a heated floor Date Issued: May 2024 Page 1 of 3 Purpose To provide an alternative solution for providing adequate insulation value below a heated floor in contact with the ground. Discussion The objective of insulation below a heated floor in contact with the ground is to reduce the environmental impact due to heat transmission to the ground from the heated floor. Section 9.36. of the National Building Code – 2023 Alberta Edition (NBC(AE)) ensures this objective is achieved. However, this code provision impacts the viability of hydronic heating systems in floors in contact with the ground. Hydronic heat is an energy efficient method for heating a home that uses tubing to run a hot liquid in the floor, along base board heaters or through radiators to heat your home. Also referred to as radiant heating, this type of system has become increasingly popular in Alberta for homeowners who want added comfort and control in their heating zones, savings through lower heating bills, and a decrease in their environmental impact by making smart green building choices. Current under slab-insulation code provisions do not take into account hydronic heating systems as an appropriate method of adequate insulation value below a heated floor in contact with the ground. Municipal Affairs identified that the provisions for current slab-insulation are more than what is required to meet energy efficiency objectives and is consulting with the National Research Council (NRC) to recommend an appropriate insulation rating that will allow for hydronic heating installations while also supporting Alberta’s energy efficiency goals. This province-wide variance will allow an alternative solution to the provisions under Section 9.36. for use in installations below heated floors in contact with

the ground. It is important to note, this variance will not remove the insulation requirement from Section 9.36. of NBC(AE), but the variance will allow, as an alternative, less than the RSI 2.84 (R-16) of under-slab insulation where hydronic or radiant floor heating is installed in the province. Background information • An energy performance analysis conducted on a “typical” constructed home in Alberta demonstrated a reduction in energy consumption when an RSI 0.88 (R 5) insulation below a heated floor is increased to an RSI 1.32 (R 7.5) insulation, providing a 30% increase in thermal performance. In the event a project is aiming for a high-performance energy target, the energy performance analysis demonstrated that increasing the insulation below a heated floor above RSI 1.32 (R 7.5) has marginal impacts on comfort and total annual energy consumption. Building STANDATA | Alberta.ca ©2024 Government of Alberta | May 2024 | Municipal Affairs STANDATA variance 23-BCV-004 Building Sprinkler-protected glazing in fire-resistant wall assemblies Date Issued: May 2024 Page 1 of 3 Purpose To set conditions where the use of sprinkler-protected glazing assemblies in interior and exterior fire rated wall assemblies is acceptable. Discussion Sentence 3.1.7.1.(1) of the National Building Code - 2023 Alberta Edition (NBC(AE)) specifies the fire-resistance rating of a material, assembly, or structural component must be determined by testing to CAN/ULC-S101, “Standard Method of Fire Endurance Tests of Building Construction and Materials.” Designers want to install clear glass in fire separations and exit enclosures to provide greater visibility within the building. Glass block and wired glass panels do not provide the visibility that designers would like to incorporate into their designs. As such, an alternative to using glass block and wired glass panels has been requested by stakeholders. Sprinkler-protected glazing is a design alternative that has been in use for years. It varies slightly from the concept of using glass block and wired glass panels. Sprinkler-protected glazing is not considered as a closure in a fire- rated assembly. Instead, the fire-resistance rating assigned to the combination of glazing assembly and sprinkler heads must be able to achieve at least the same fire-resistance rating of the fire separation it is being installed within. ULC-S101 does not contain requirements that adequately address sprinkler-protected glazing. Since the sprinkler-protected glazing is used as an alternative to the traditional fire-rated assembly, the installation of the sprinkler-protected glazing panels does not reduce the number of unprotected openings permitted in a given exterior wall assembly. Consequently, glazing assemblies are permitted to be installed for interior or exterior fire rated assemblies required to have a fire-resistance rating without being tested to CAN/ULC-S101 as required by

Sentences 3.1.7.1.(1) and 9.10.3.1.(1) provided they are protected by a fixed, automatic sprinkler system and the criteria of this variance are followed. Underwriter’s Laboratories Canada has published CAN/ULC-S136:2021, “Standard Method of Fire Test for Sprinkler Protected Window Systems”. Code References Sentence 3.1.7.1.(1) 3.1.7.1. Determination of Ratings 1) Except as permitted by Sentence (2) and Articles 3.1.7.2. and 3.6.3.5., the rating of a material, assembly of materials or a structural member that is required to have a fire-resistance rating, shall be determined on the basis of the results of tests conducted in conformance with CAN/ULC-S101, “Standard Method of Fire Endurance Tests of Building Construction and Materials.” STANDATA 23-BCV-004 Page 2 of 3 Building STANDATA | Alberta.ca ©2024 Government of Alberta | May 2024 | Municipal Affairs Sentence 9.10.3.1.(1) 9.10.3.1. Fire-Resistance and Fire-Protection Ratings 1) Where a fire-resistance rating or a fire-protection rating is required in this Section for an element of a building, such rating shall be determined in conformance with a) the test methods described in Part 3, b) the calculation method presented in Appendix D, or c) the construction specifications presented in Tables 9.10.3.1.-A and 9.10.3.1.-B. Sentence 3.2.4.1.(1) 3.2.4.1. Determination of Requirement for a Fire Alarm System 1) Except as permitted in Sentences (2) and (3), a fire alarm system shall be installed in buildings in which an automatic sprinkler system is installed. Sentence 3.2.5.12.(1) 3.2.5.12. Automatic Sprinkler Systems 1) Except as permitted by Sentences (2) to (4) and (9), an automatic sprinkler system shall be designed, constructed, installed and tested in conformance with NFPA 13, “Standard for the Installation of Sprinkler Systems.” (See Note A-3.2.5.12.(1).) Variance This variance provides approximately equivalent or greater safety performance with respect to persons and property as provided for by the Safety Codes Act and the NBC(AE). Glazing assemblies are permitted to be

installed for interior or exterior fire rated assemblies that are required to have a fire-resistance rating without being tested to CAN/ULC-S101, “Standard Method of Fire Endurance Tests of Building Construction and Materials” as required by Sentences 3.1.7.1.(1) and 9.10.3.1.(1) provided they are protected by a fixed, automatic sprinkler system and the following criteria are met: 1. The assembly has been evaluated by a testing agency accredited by the Standards Council of Canada for conformance to CAN/ULC-S136:2021, “Standard Method of Fire Test for Sprinkler Protected Window Systems”. 2. The design, construction and installation of automatic sprinkler system conforms to NFPA 13. 3. Sprinklers are listed as specific application window sprinklers. 4. Glazing is heat-strengthened, tempered, or glass ceramic and fixed. 5. Where the assembly is required to be protected from both sides, sprinklers to be installed on both sides of the glazing. 6. If the assembly is located in a loadbearing assembly, all loadbearing components have a fire-resistance rating not less than that required for the supported assembly. 7. The glazed assembly does not include any horizontal members interfering with uniform distribution of water over the surface of the glazing, and there are no obstructions between sprinklers and glazing that would obstruct water distribution. 8. The fire-resistance rating of the sprinkler-protected glazing system is equal to or greater than the fire- resistance rating required for the wall assembly being installed within, and the sprinkler-protected glazed wall assemblies constructed according to the requirements of the listing of the window sprinkler. STANDATA 23-BCV-004 Page 3 of 3 Building STANDATA | Alberta.ca ©2024 Government of Alberta | May 2024 | Municipal Affairs 9. The assembly is not installed in: • a firewall or within a door installed in a firewall, • a building that contains a high hazard industrial occupancy, • a location where

there is a risk of explosion, or • any part of a required exit serving: - a floor area subjected to the additional requirements for high buildings as per Subsection 3.2.6., - a care, treatment or detention occupancy, or - a residential occupancy. 10. Where the assembly is installed in exits not mentioned in criteria (9.) above, the exits do not comprise more than one half of the required number of exits from any floor area. 11. The window sprinkler system: • Is identified at the isolation valve as supplying a window sprinkler system. • Is provided with a placard adjacent to the incoming water service with the following wording: “SPECIAL WINDOW SPRINKLER HEADS ON THIS SYSTEM ARE AN INTEGRAL PART OF THE FIRE SEPARATIONS. THIS WATER SUPPLY MAY ONLY BE SHUT OFF AFTER ALL THE PROPER AUTHORITIES HAVE RECEIVED NOTICE IN WRITING”. - Font size to be 12mm high. - Placard to be ‘RED’ in colour with white lettering. - Mount to existing wall with appropriate anchors. - Adhesive is not acceptable. • Provides a water supply duration for the design area that includes the window sprinklers but not less than the required fire resistance rating of the assembly. Notes: 1. As with all fire protection measures, care to be exercised in the design, installation, and maintenance of the active fire protection system to ensure its reliability throughout the life of the building. 2. Sprinkler-protected glazing may be used as a protected opening in an exposing building face where sprinkler heads are provided only on the interior side of the glazing. 3. Sprinkler-protected glazing may be used in an interior fire separation if sprinkler heads are provided to protect both sides of the glazing. 4. Sprinkler-protected glazing may be used in a sprinklered or an unsprinklered building. The installation of sprinkler-protected glazing will also require the installation of a fire alarm system for the building, as required by Sentence 3.2.4.1.(1). Building STANDATA | Alberta.ca ©2024 Government of Alberta | Published: May 2024 | Municipal Affairs STANDATA variance 23-BCV-005 Building Occupancy classification of oil and gas processing buildings Date Issued: May 2024 Page 1 of 3 Purpose To allow oil and gas Group F, Division 1 hig- hazard industrial occupancies to be classified as Group F, Division 2 medium-hazard occupancy under certain conditions as an alternative solution under the National Building Code - 2023 Alberta Edition (NBC(AE)). Discussion Oil and gas processing buildings are often classified as Group F, Division 1, high-hazard industrial occupancies thus requiring these sites to comply with more restrictive provisions. In oil and gas facilities, the work environment, safe work procedures, and worker safety training is an important complement to the building’s fire protection and suppression systems. Oil and gas companies have developed guides describing design and operation practices that support safe working conditions at small, portable oil and gas production facilities, often classified as high hazard industrial occupancies. The objective of these guides is to limit the probability that a person in or adjacent to a facility may be exposed to an unacceptable level of risk of injury or illness. The Canadian Association of Petroleum Producers (CAPP) recently produced “Safety Guidelines for Small, Portable Oil and Gas Production Facilities: Recommended Solutions for Design and Operations”. The guide is intended to supplement other applicable standards and regulatory codes including the NBC(AE). It recommends solutions for safe design, operation, and maintenance practices for field facilities including worker training and competency. There are three main areas of focus: process safety, public safety, and occupational health and safety. Owners should assess their own requirements to establish design, operating, maintenance, and work. Municipal Affairs reviewed the CAPP guide and found the implementation of the recommended guidelines, in addition to other safety

conditions described in this variance, may allow for some oil and gas processing buildings to be classified as Group F, Division 2 medium-hazard occupancies. Building STANDATA | Alberta.ca ©2024 Government of Alberta | Published: May 2024 | Municipal Affairs STANDATA variance 23-BCV-006 Building Occupancy classification of natural gas regulating and metering buildings Date Issued: May 2024 Page 1 of 2 Purpose To provide an alternative solution for occupancy classification of Group F, Division 1 high-hazard industrial occupancies that house natural gas and metering equipment to be classified as Group F, Division 2 medium- hazard occupancy under certain conditions. Discussion High Hazard Industrial Occupancy (Group F, Division 1) is defined by the National Building Code - 2023 Alberta Edition (NBC(AE)) as an industrial occupancy containing sufficient quantities of highly combustible, flammable or explosive materials which, because of their inherent characteristics, may constitute a special fire hazard. Buildings containing natural gas regulating and metering equipment are typically designed to protect the equipment. These buildings are not accessible by the public and are only intended for occupancy by employees for maintenance so the risk of harm to the public is lower than other buildings. Such features allow for accepting Group F, Division 2 medium-hazard occupancy as an alternative occupancy classification. Code References Sentence 6.3.1.5.(1) 6.3.1.5. Indoor Air Contaminants (See Note A-6.3.1.5.) 1) Air contaminants of concern that are released within buildings shall a) be removed insofar as is possible at their points of origin, and b) not be permitted to accumulate in concentrations greater than those permitted by applicable provincial or territorial requirements or, in the absence of such requirements, by good engineering practice such as that described in the publications listed in Sentence 6.2.1.1.(1), measured using the methodology described therein. Division A, Article 1.4.1.2. 1.4.1.2. Defined Terms High-hazard industrial occupancy (Group F, Division 1) means an industrial occupancy containing sufficient quantities of highly combustible and flammable or explosive materials which, because of their inherent characteristics, constitute

a special fire hazard. Medium-hazard industrial occupancy (Group F, Division 2) means an industrial occupancy in which the combustible content is more than 50 kg/m2 or 1 200 MJ/m2 of floor area and not classified as a high- hazard industrial occupancy. Building STANDATA | Alberta.ca ©2024 Government of Alberta | June 2024 | Municipal Affairs STANDATA variance 23-BCV-008 Building Residential exhaust outlet clearance from air intakes Date Issued: June 2024 Page 1 of 3 Purpose To provide an alternative solution to clearance requirements between domestic kitchen, bathroom and clothes dryer exhaust outlets from air intakes. Discussion The requirements for exhaust clearances from soffits were updated in the National Building Code of Canada 2020 and subsequently harmonized within the National Building Code - 2023 Alberta Edition (NBC(AE)). The requirements prescribed a clearance of 1800 mm from exhaust vents below soffits or to install solid soffits where the clearance is less than 1800 mm below soffits. Clearance was increased from 900 mm to 1800 mm for clothes dryer exhaust vents to air intakes. This change did not differentiate between clothes dryers in common laundry rooms serving residential buildings or domestic clothes dryers serving a single dwelling unit or a house with a secondary suite. Clearance of 1800 mm was also added for bathroom ventilation exhaust from air intakes. The rationale presented within the requirements for exhaust clearances explained the application to soffits but did not provide a rationale applicable to clothes dryer exhaust or bathroom exhaust from air intakes. The rationale also describes “air containing moisture rises from the exhaust outlets” as part of the problem. The rationale was silent on kitchen exhaust from dwelling units. But to clarify are also addressing kitchen exhaust outlets. Kitchen, bathroom, and clothes dryer exhaust serving individual dwelling units or houses with a secondary suite typically operate intermittently. CSA-B149.1 “Natural gas and propane installation code” (CSA B149.1) provides for vent terminations from building air intakes prescribing a clearance of 900 mm for domestic clothes dryers and 1800 mm for commercial clothes dryers. This supports the allowance for

the clearance reduction when dealing with domestic clothes dryers. The domestic clothes dryer exhaust air would typically contain more moisture than bathroom exhaust air. Code References Sentences, 9.32.3.13.(4)(5)(6) 9.32.3.13. Outdoor Intake and Exhaust Openings 4) Except as provided in Sentences (5) and (6), exhaust outlets that discharge air containing moisture, such as bathroom ventilation and clothes dryer exhaust outlets, shall be located at least 1 800 mm from air intakes and vented soffits. Archived STANDATA 23-BCV-008 Page 2 of 3 Building STANDATA | Alberta.ca ©2024 Government of Alberta | June 2024 | Municipal Affairs 5) Where an exhaust outlet referred to in Sentence (4) is located within a soffit, the soffit shall either be unvented, or if vented, the full depth of the soffit shall be blocked for a distance of 1 800 mm on each side of the exhaust outlet. 6) Where an exhaust outlet referred to in Sentence (4) is located in a sidewall less than 1 800 mm from a soffit, a section of the soffit above the exhaust outlet shall be unvented, or if vented, the full depth of the soffit shall be blocked in accordance with the widths stipulated in Table 9.32.3.13.-A, centred over the location of the outlet. CSA-B149.1 Sentences 7.5.1 and 7.5.2 7.5 Domestic-type clothes dryers 7.5.1 A dryer shall be equipped with a moisture-exhaust duct that terminates outside the building, and the duct shall be constructed of a material that is (a) noncombustible; or (b) certified as meeting the requirements for Class 1 air ducts contained in CAN/ULC-S110. 7.5.2 A moisture-exhaust duct shall not terminate within 3 ft (1 m) in any direction of any pressure regulator vent termination or fresh-air intake. CSA-B149.1 Clause 8.14.8 (c) 8.14.8 A vent shall not terminate c) within 6 ft (1.8 m) of a mechanical air-supply

inlet to any building; Rationale for Clearance change Problem Exhaust from clothes dryers and bathroom fans is allowed to discharge from vents installed in the soffits and in the side walls below the soffits. This warm, moist air can enter the attic space through any vented soffits in the immediate vicinity of the exhaust vent, potentially causing mold, mildew, rot, loss of the insulation’s R-value, ice damming, and water infiltration. Approximately 5% of houses with soffit exhaust vents conforming to the current code requirements show signs of mold, mildew, rot, and water infiltration. Rationale Installing unvented soffits or blocking a section of vented soffits for a certain width on each side of exhaust vents will prevent the infiltration of warm, moist air from the exhaust vents into the attic space, which can cause mold, mildew, rot, loss of the insulation’s R-value, ice damming, and water infiltration. Air containing moisture rises from the exhaust outlets and infiltrates the attic through the soffits, then condensation builds up in the attic over time, resulting in the growth of mold, which causes the deterioration of the ceiling below the roof. Most homeowners do not realize that the roof sheathing on their house is rotting until they replace the roof or notice mold on an interior finish—mold that could be affecting the health of the occupants. Application This variance applies to kitchen, bathroom, and clothes dryer exhaust outlets serving individual dwelling units or a house with a secondary

suite. Variance This variance provides approximately equivalent or greater safety performance with respect to persons and property as provided for by the Safety Codes Act and the NBC(AE). 1. The horizontal clearance of kitchen, bathroom and clothes dryer exhaust outlets is permitted to be within 900 mm from air intakes serving the individual dwelling unit or house with a secondary suite. Building STANDATA | Alberta.ca ©2024 Government of Alberta | October 2024 | Municipal Affairs STANDATA variance 23-BCV-008(REV1) Building Residential exhaust outlet clearance from air intakes Date Issued: October 2024 Page 1 of 4 Purpose Provides an alternative solution to Sentence 9.32.3.13.(4) for the minimum clearance requirement for domestic exhaust outlets that discharge air containing moisture, such as kitchen, bathroom, and clothes dryer exhaust outlets, from air intakes. Discussion The National Building Code of Canada 2020 introduced changes to Article 9.32.3.13. for minimum clearance requirements related to exhaust vents, soffits, and air intakes. The National Building Code – 2023 Alberta Edition (NBC(AE)) subsequently harmonized with these changes. The minimum clearance required between a gas vent or oil fill pipe and a mechanically vented air intake was increased from 900 mm to 1 800 mm in Sentence 9.32.3.13.(3). Additionally, new Sentences (4) to (6) were introduced to address the minimum clearance required from exhaust outlets discharging moisture-laden air to soffits and air intakes. While the national code change rationale for Sentences (4) to (6) specifically explained the application of the 1 800 mm minimum clearance requirement to soffits, it did not address the application to air intakes as provided in Sentence (4). A required 1 800 mm minimum clearance between moist-air exhaust outlets and air intakes for domestic applications was not explained and other standards suggest it can be potentially reduced. CSA-B149.1, “Natural gas and propane installation code,” (CSA B149.1) provides minimum clearances between clothes dryer vent terminations and air intakes: 900 mm for domestic clothes dryers and 1 800 mm for commercial clothes dryers. As domestic clothes dryer exhaust air typically contains more moisture than bathroom or kitchen exhaust air, this supports the basis for a variance that reduces the 1 800 mm minimum required clearance between a moist-air exhaust outlet

and air intake specified by Sentence 9.32.3.13.(4) of the NBC(AE). As air intakes located above moist-air exhaust outlets are more susceptible to the effects of infiltration (due to the rising of warm, moist air), the reduction in the required minimum clearance from 1 800 mm to 900 mm provided in this variance is only applicable to where the moist-air exhaust outlet is located horizontally to the air intake or above it. This maintains the rationale for the changes to Article 9.32.3.13. in the NBC(AE) while providing appropriate reductions in the required minimum clearance for certain dimensions (see Figure A). Air intakes specified by Sentence (4) refer to intakes supplying ventilation air to the building and includes those connected to HRV’s/ERV’s or the return air plenum of a furnace. Note that in cases where the fresh air intake connected to the return air plenum of a furnace is less than 8 inches in diameter, it can be considered as a “building opening” rather than an air intake (as the CSA B149.1 standard also allows for). Moist-air exhaust outlets specified by Sentence (4) include not only bathroom ventilation and clothes dryer exhaust outlets, but kitchen exhaust outlets as well, despite kitchen exhaust outlets not being explicitly mentioned in the Sentence itself or in the rationale for the code change. Building STANDATA | Alberta.ca ©2024 Government of Alberta | October 2024 | Municipal Affairs STANDATA variance 23-BCV-009 Building CSA B52:23 Mechanical refrigeration code Date Issued: October 2024 Page 1 of 2 Purpose Allows the acceptance of CSA B52:23, “Mechanical refrigeration code,” under the National Building Code – 2023 Alberta Edition (NBC(AE)). Discussion On January 1, 2025, new standards for manufacturing with refrigerants will go into effect. These standards include prohibiting the manufacture of products containing certain hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs) by January 1, 2025. HFCs are synthetic organic compounds used in air conditioning and as refrigerants. To conform to these rule changes, the 2023 edition of the CSA B52 code introduced the A2L and B2L refrigerant groups as more environmentally friendly refrigerants. Equipment manufacturers have also begun to adapt to the rule changes by re-tooling their factories to manufacture new equipment to allow for the use of these A2L and B2L refrigerant groups. Additionally, there is already equipment on the market which use the new refrigerants. The NBC(AE), however, currently references the 2018 edition of the CSA B52 Code, as per Table 1.3.1.2. of Division B. To align with the HFC prohibition and industry’s change in supply of HVAC equipment across Canada, it is necessary for the NBC(AE) to recognize the CSA B52:23 Code. Building STANDATA | Alberta.ca ©2025 Government of Alberta | February 2025 | Municipal Affairs STANDATA variance 23-BCV-010 Building Engineer authentication for the qualification of structural steel fabricators Date Issued: February 2025 Page 1 of 5 Purpose To provide an alternative solution to the industry in meeting the requirement of using qualified fabricators for the fabrication of structural steel as per CSA W47.1 – “Certification of companies for fusion welding of steel”. Discussion Structural steel is at times fabricated outside of Canada by fabricators who are not certified to the CSA W47.1 standard. The majority of fabricators in Canada are certified to the CSA W47.1 standard. However, it is not common to find CSA W47.1 qualified fabricators outside of Canada. The standard commonly adopted by the international community of fabricators involved in the fabrication and welding of structural steel is AWS D1.1 “Structural Welding Code–Steel”. The Canadian equivalent standard to AWS D1.1 is CSA W59 “Welded steel construction” (metal arc welding). The two standards are quite similar in the welding requirements. The CSA W47.1 “Certification of companies for fusion welding of steel”, is associated with CSA W59, which provides certification requirements to structural steel fabricators. However, there is no equivalent standard to complement CSA W47.1 since the industry relies on fabricators’ own quality programs to comply with the AWS D1.1 requirements during welding activities. The National Building Code – 2023 Alberta Edition (NBC(AE)) mandates the use of CSA S16 “Design of steel structures” and Canadian Welding Bureau (CWB) certification. The requirement to comply with CSA W47.1 stems from CSA S16 (refer to Clause 24.3) which is mandated by the NBC(AE). In scenarios which involve fabricators outside of Canada due to limitations of access to CWB certified companies, allowance should be made available for industry to utilize this variance. This variance provides

an analysis of AWS D1.1 as an alternative solution recommendation for instances where CWB certified fabricators are not available. A variance involving the practice of engineering is also a matter for the Association of Professional Engineers and Geoscientists of Alberta (APEGA) to take into consideration, as the practice of engineering is a self-regulated profession governed by APEGA. The references to APEGA’s authentication standard as a condition of this variance is a substantive basis for this variance providing approximately equivalent or greater safety performance. Building STANDATA | Alberta.ca ©2025 Government of Alberta | February 2025 | Municipal Affairs Mina and Plau STANDATA variance 23-BCV-011 Building Polyethylene film for greenhouse enclosures Date Issued: February 2025 Page 1 of 2 Purpose This variance allows the use of products specifically designed for commercial greenhouse facilities occupied only by greenhouse staff, where members of the public are not permitted access. Discussion Flame-resistant fabrics and films conforming to CAN/ULC-S109, “Standard Method for Flame Tests of Flame- Resistant Fabrics and Films” are designed to be used for tents and air-supported structures within the scope of the National Building Code - 2023 Alberta Edition (NBC(AE)). Use of such materials for commercial greenhouses would be detrimental to plants due to the material’s ability to block out the majority of the ultraviolet light necessary for plant growth. For commercial greenhouse facilities, several types of polyethylene films with special additives for greenhouse use are available but do not meet the CAN/ULC-S109 criteria. Flame Resistance 1) Every tent and air-supported structure and all tarpaulins and decorative materials used in connection with these structures shall conform to CAN/ULC-S109, “Standard Method for Flame Tests of Flame- Resistant Fabrics and Films.” Application This variance applies to commercial greenhouse facilities not intended for the public. Variance This variance provides approximately equivalent or greater safety performance with respect to persons and property as provided for by the Safety Codes Act and the (NBC(AE)). Polyethylene film used to enclose commercial greenhouse facilities is not required to conform to CAN/ULC-S109, “Standard Method for Flame Tests of Flame-Resistant Fabrics and Films,” under the following conditions: 1. the greenhouse is used only for the growing of plants, (flowers, vegetables, shrubs, trees, etc.), 2. members of the public do not have access to the greenhouse, and 3. the polyethylene film

has a flame spread rating not exceeding 25. Building STANDATA | Alberta.ca ©2026 Government of Alberta | October 2026 | Municipal Affairs STANDATA variance 23-BCV-011R1 Building Polyethylene film for greenhouse enclosures Date Issued: October 2026 Page 1 of 2 Purpose To allow the use of products specifically designed for commercial greenhouse facilities. This variance establishes conditions under which polyethylene film may be used in greenhouses occupied by greenhouse staff only, and under certain circumstances, in greenhouses that allow public access. Discussion Flame-resistant fabrics conforming to CAN/ULC-S109, “Standard Method for Flame Tests of Flame-Resistant Fabrics and Films,” are intended for use in tents and air-supported structures. Use of such materials for commercial greenhouses may be detrimental to plant growth due to their ability to reduce the transmission of ultraviolet light required for healthy plant development. Several types of polyethylene films specifically manufactured for greenhouse applications are available in the marketplace. These products incorporate additives designed to optimize plant growth and environmental performance but generally do not conform to the requirements of CAN/ULC-S109. Code References Article 3.1.18.5. 3.1.18.5. Flame Resistance 1) Every tent and air-supported structure and all tarpaulins and decorative materials used in connection with these structures shall conform to CAN/ULC-S109, “Standard Method for Flame Tests of Flame- Resistant Fabrics and Films.” Application This variance applies to commercial greenhouse facilities that fall under the application of the National Building Code – 2023 Alberta Edition (NBC(AE)). Variance This variance provides approximately equivalent or greater safety performance with respect to persons and property as provided for by the Safety Codes Act and the NBC(AE). Polyethylene film used to enclose commercial greenhouse facilities is not required to conform to CAN/ULC-S109, “Standard Method for Flame Tests of Flame-Resistant Fabrics and Films,” under the conditions of the following two options: STANDATA 23-BCV-011R1 Page 2 of 2 Building STANDATA | Alberta.ca ©2026 Government of Alberta

| October 2026 | Municipal Affairs Option 1 – Greenhouses Not Open to the Public 1. The greenhouse is used only for the growing of plants (flowers, vegetables, shrubs, trees, etc.); 2. Members of the public do not have access to the greenhouse; and 3. The polyethylene film is not required to conform to CAN/ULC-S109, “Standard Method for Flame Tests of Flame-Resistant Fabrics,” provided that it has a flame spread rating not exceeding 25. Option 2 – Greenhouses with Public Access 1. The greenhouse is one storey in building height and primarily used for the growing, display, and retail sale of plants (flowers, vegetables, shrubs, trees, and similar horticultural products); 2. The building is classified as a Group F, Division 3 major occupancy (low-hazard industrial occupancy); 3. Public access is limited to retail activities directly related to the sale of plants and horticultural products; 4. The polyethylene film is not required to conform to CAN/ULC-S109, “Standard Method for Flame Tests of Flame-Resistant Fabrics,” if it has a flame spread rating not exceeding 25; 5. Public access aisles have a clear width of not less than 1.1 m and be arranged to provide access to exits in at least two directions of travel, with no dead-end aisles; 6. Exit doors serving publicly accessible areas are increased in width by not less than 40% above the minimum width required by the NBC(AE) but not less than 1190 mm; 7. Occupant load is calculated using 4.6 m² per person for areas accessible to the public; 8. Every exit door is provided with exit signage in accordance with the NBC(AE); 9. Spatial separation and exposure protection comply with the NBC(AE). Where more than one greenhouse is located on the same property, the spatial separation between greenhouses may be determined in accordance with the provisions

applicable to tents and air-supported structures (Subsection 3.1.18.); and 10. A Fire Safety Plan must be prepared, implemented, and maintained in accordance with the National Fire Code – 2023 Alberta Edition. The Fire Safety Plan must address emergency procedures, evacuation procedures, staff responsibilities, fire protection and life safety systems, maintenance requirements, and emergency contact information. Where required by the building or fire authority having jurisdiction, the Fire Safety Plan must be submitted for review and approval prior to occupancy. For greenhouses that do not comply with either Option 1 or Option 2, the enclosing materials must conform to CAN/ULC-S109, “Standard Method for Flame Tests of Flame-Resistant Fabrics and Films,” as required by Article 3.1.18.5. This VARIANCE is applicable throughout the Province of Alberta. Building STANDATA | Alberta.ca ©2025 Government of Alberta | May 2025 | Municipal Affairs STANDATA variance 23-BCV-012R1 Building Permanent wood foundations with mechanically laminated timber panels for Part 9 residential buildings Date Issued: May 2025 Page 1 of 2 Purpose To permit permanent wood foundations made from mechanically laminated timber panels (MLTP) as detailed within the document “Permanent Wood Foundations with Mechanically Laminated Timber Panels for Part 9 Residential Buildings in Alberta” (the document), as an alternative solution under the National Building Code – 2023 Alberta Edition (NBC(AE)). Discussion Sentence 9.15.2.4.(1) of Division B of the NBC(AE) contains requirements for permanent wood foundations in buildings designed in compliance with Part 9. Clause 9.15.2.4.(1)(a) permits permanent wood foundations if the foundation conforms to CSA S406-16 “Specification of permanent wood foundations for housing and small buildings.” MLTP are not included within the scope of the CSA S406-16 standard. Therefore, permanent wood foundations made from MLTP would have to comply with Clause 9.15.2.4.(1)(b) of Division B which indicates the foundation is to conform to Part 4. Sentence 2.4.1.2.(1) of Division C requires designs in accordance with Part 4 to be carried out by a registered professional skilled in the work concerned. Sentence 2.4.1.2.(2) of Division C requires a registered professional to perform field reviews of preserved wood foundations designed in accordance to Part 4. The document supplements the CSA S406-16 standard and provides pre-engineered structural designs for MLTP for permanent wood foundations. This permits permanent wood foundations made from MLTP designed in compliance with the document to fall within the scope of Clause 9.15.2.4.(1)(a) of the NBC(AE). Building STANDATA | Alberta.ca ©2025 Government of Alberta | March 2025 | Municipal Affairs STANDATA variance 23-BCV-014 Building Multi-level storage racking systems Date Issued: March 2025 Page 1 of 5 Purpose To allow an alternative solution for multi-level storage racking systems to be considered as special and unusual structures under the National Building Code – 2023 Alberta Edition (NBC(AE)). The NBC(AE) contains no specific requirements for multi-level storage racking systems. Manufacturers of these types of structures have requested they be considered as special and unusual structures according to Article 3.2.2.2. and be designed according to good fire protection engineering practice. Discussion Multi-level storage racking systems have distinctive features which distinguish these systems from high-rack storage systems. In traditional high-rack storage systems, access to the commodities is provided by means of ladders or robotic material handling systems. Multi-level storage racking systems, however, have intermediate work platforms designed to enable access to the stored commodities without the use of ladders. Various Safety Codes Officers (SCOs) have interpreted the design of the multi-level storage racking systems as equivalent to individual storeys, mezzanines or interconnected floor spaces. While this interpretation can be supported by the NBC(AE), the low occupant loads and the restriction on access to only to authorized personnel to areas housing these systems allows for an alternative assessment as special and unusual structures. Specific conditions related to fire safety plans, fire prevention, protection and suppression, egress, signage and lighting and emergency power systems are necessary to be in place to support an assessment of these systems as special and unusual structures. Parts 3 and 4 of the National Fire Code – 2023 Alberta Edition (NFC(AE)) contain provisions for the storage of products that may affect the design of the storage racking system, therefore it is highly recommended to solicit the input of

local fire prevention and/or fire department personnel prior to applying for a building permit to construct a multi-level storage racking system. Please refer to the following publications for additional information on good fire protection engineering principles related to time-based egress analysis, occupant behavior during fire conditions and emergency movement of building occupants: • “The SFPE Handbook of Fire Protection Engineering, Fourth Edition”, published by Springer (ISBN 978- 0877658214) as referenced in the NFC(AE) DEFINED TERMS The words and terms in italics in this STANDATA have the following meanings that are specific to this STANDATA only and are not intended to be used in other contexts: Access level means an intermediate walkway within a multi-level storage racking system for personnel access. Multi-level storage racking system means a self-supporting structural facility within a building having one or more intermediate access levels. Building STANDATA | Alberta.ca ©2025 Government of Alberta | September 2025 | Municipal Affairs STANDATA variance 23-BCV-017 Building Unvented roof assembly Date Issued: September 2025 Page 1 of 2 Purpose This variance sets out the conditions for a safety codes officer (SCO) to accept the use of an unvented roof assembly under Part 9 of the National Building Code – 2023 Alberta Edition (NBC(AE)). Discussion Currently, the NBC(AE) allows unvented roof assemblies referring the reader to the Note for further guidance. Sentence 9.19.1.1.(1) suggests there are some types of roof assemblies where venting is not necessary, with the wording “Except where it can be shown to be unnecessary…” and goes on to refer the reader to Note A- 9.19.1.1.(1) for specific examples of assemblies where venting is not required. The Note indicates that “The exception provided in Article 9.19.1.1. recognizes for some specialized ceiling-roof assemblies, ventilation would not be required.” Elsewhere in Section 9.19. other roof assemblies are identified as not requiring venting. Sentence 9.19.1.4.(1) indicates “The lower portion of a mansard or gambrel style roof need not be ventilated.” Code References Sentence 9.19.1.1.(1) Sentence 9.19.1.4.(1) 9.19.1.4. Mansard or Gambrel Roof 1) The lower portion of a mansard or gambrel style roof need not be ventilated. 9.19.1.1. Required Venting 1) Except where it can be shown to be unnecessary, where insulation is installed between a ceiling and the underside of the roof sheathing, a space shall be provided between the insulation and the sheathing, and vents shall be installed to permit the transfer of moisture from the space to the exterior. (See Note A- 9.19.1.1.(1).) A-9.19.1.1.(1) Venting of Attic or Roof Spaces. Controlling the flow of moisture by air leakage and vapour diffusion into attic or roof spaces is necessary to limit moisture-induced deterioration. Given that imperfections normally exist in

the vapour barriers and air barrier systems, recent research indicates that venting of attic or roof spaces is generally still required. The exception provided in Article 9.19.1.1. recognizes that some specialized ceiling-roof assemblies, such as those used in some factory-built buildings, have, over time, demonstrated that their construction is sufficiently tight to prevent excessive moisture accumulation. In these cases, ventilation would not be required. STANDATA 23-BCV-017 Page 2 of 2 Building STANDATA | Alberta.ca ©2025 Government of Alberta | September 2025 | Municipal Affairs Application Roof assemblies in Part 9 residential buildings. Building codes and standards | Alberta.ca ©2025 Government of Alberta | September 2025 | Municipal Affairs STANDATA variance 23-BCV-018 Building Vented soffit protection Date Issued: September 2025 Page 1 of 4 Purpose This variance provides an alternative solution for the protection of soffits where typical vented soffit materials are otherwise not permitted. Discussion Sentences 9.10.14.5.(12), 9.10.15.5.(11) and 9.10.12.4.(2) and (3) of the National Building Code – 2023 Alberta Edition (NBC(AE)) require soffits in areas of concern to have no openings and be protected by specific thicknesses of sheet steel, aluminum, gypsum board, OSB, plywood or lumber to provide a higher level of fire protection. Having to provide solid (unvented) soffits in lieu of vented ones in areas of concern means designers must achieve the ventilation required at the roof space’s lower end(s) via alternative means. Although viewed as unideal by most designers, builders and owners, this is commonly accomplished by installing surface roof vents in the area of the lower ends of the roof space. With the use of a material comprised of an intumescent coating on a vented substrate, it is possible to provide ventilation to a roof space through the soffit area, while simultaneously providing fire protection that meets or exceeds NBC(AE) requirements where openings in soffits are not permitted. The material is fastened to the underside of roof or floor projections, and a finished vented soffit material can be installed to cover it for aesthetic purposes. When elevated temperatures are present due to a fire, the intumescent coating expands to seal the openings within the vented substrate. Code References Sentence 9.10.14.5.(12) 9.10.14.5.
